h: A steam engine, an overhead railway and the Beatles' city
p: One of the first things to catch your eye is Lion, an early steam locomotive built in 1838 for the Liverpool and Manchester Railway. It's a gorgeous piece of engineering, and it later starred in the classic Ealing comedy The Titfield Thunderbolt. Nearby, a carriage from the Liverpool Overhead Railway, nicknamed the 'Dockers' Umbrella', recalls the elevated line that once ran along the docks until it closed in the 1950s.

Galleries cover everything from the city's growth as a global port to its music, sport and communities. The Wondrous Place gallery celebrates Liverpool's culture, with plenty of nods to the Beatles and the city's footballing rivalry, while other spaces dig into how people from all over the world made Liverpool their home. For the very youngest visitors, Little Liverpool is a dedicated space for under-sixes, with plenty to play with and explore.
Admission is free, so you can easily pop in for an hour or make it a longer visit. Big windows in the building frame cracking views of the Three Graces and the Mersey, so keep an eye out as you go.

The museum is perfectly placed for a day on the waterfront. Outside, the Beatles statue at the Pier Head is a must for a photo, and the Mersey Ferries leave from just nearby for a trip across the river. The Royal Albert Dock houses the Merseyside Maritime Museum and the International Slavery Museum, both a short walk along the river and well worth adding on.
